$$

$$
f(x)=x\iff g(x)=0
$$

has exactly one solution; $f$ is a strict contraction on ${\mathbf R}$
and the fixed point is unique.  In the usual form this is the
Banach–Caccioppoli fixed point on the whole line.

constant $a=1$.  Then (1) is $|g(x)-g(y)|>0$ and $g$ is only injective.

so that on $\mathcal F_{t-1}=\sigma(\mu_{0},\sigma_{0}^{2},\ldots ,\mu_{t-1},

$$
\mu_{t}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}\sim N\!\left(\mu_{t-1},\frac{\sigma_{t-1}^{2}}{n}\right),

and $\mu_{t}$ and $\sigma_{t}^{2}$ are conditionally independent. In
particular

$$
{\mathbb E}\!\left[\sigma_{t}^{2}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}\right]=\sigma_{t-1}^{2},
\qquad 
{\mathbb E}\!\left[\mu_{t}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}\right]=\mu_{t-1},
$$

so $\sigma_{t}^{2}$ and $\mu_{t}$ are non-negative martingales.  Put

$$
Y_{t}:=\frac{\sigma_{t}^{2}}{\sigma_{t-1}^{2}}=\frac{\chi^{2}_{\,n-1}}{n-1},
\qquad t\ge1,
$$

i.i.d. with ${\mathbb E}Y_{t}=1$.  Then

$$
\log\sigma_{t}^{2}=\log\sigma_{0}^{2}+\sum_{k=1}^{t}\log Y_{k},
\qquad 
{\mathbb E}\log Y_{1}<0,
$$

because $\log$ is strictly concave and ${\mathbb E}Y_{1}=1$.  Hence

$$
\frac1t\log\sigma_{t}^{2}\xrightarrow[t\to\infty]{a.s.}{\mathbb E}\log Y_{1}<0,
$$

so that

$$
\sigma_{t}^{2}\xrightarrow[t\to\infty]{a.s.}0,
$$

and in fact $\sigma_{t}^{2}=O_{a.s.}\!\left(e^{\,t{\mathbb E}\log Y_{1}}\right)$
decays geometrically.  The positive martingale $\sigma_{t}^{2}$ therefore
converges a.s., and the limit is $0$ a.s.  In particular $\mu_{t}$ is a
martingale with $\operatorname{Var}(\mu_{t}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})
=\sigma_{t-1}^{2}/n\to0$ a.s., so $\mu_{t}\to\mu_{\infty}$ a.s. as well.

Put $S_{t}=\sum_{i=0}^{t}\sigma_{i}^{2}$.  $S_{t}\uparrow S_{\infty}$ a.s.
with

$$
S_{\infty}=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\sigma_{i}^{2}<\infty\qquad\text{a.s.}
$$

because the summands decay exponentially a.s.  Hence $S_{t}\to S_{\infty}$
a.s. and in particular $S_{t}\to S_{\infty}$ in probability and in
distribution, $S_{\infty}$ being a proper non-degenerate random variable
with $S_{\infty}>0$ a.s.  Up to the harmless constant $\sigma_{0}^{2}=1$,

$$
S_{\infty}\stackrel{d}{=}\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\prod_{k=1}^{i}Y_{k},\qquad
Y_{k}\stackrel{iid}{=}\chi^{2}_{\,n-1}/(n-1),
$$

the usual geometric random series generated by a multiplicative random
walk with negative logarithmic drift.

The convergence is not $L^{1}$.  Indeed
${\mathbb E}[\sigma_{t}^{2}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=\sigma_{t-1}^{2}$ so
${\mathbb E}\sigma_{t}^{2}={\mathbb E}\sigma_{0}^{2}=1$ for every $t$ and

$$
{\mathbb E}S_{t}= \sum_{i=0}^{t}{\mathbb E}\sigma_{i}^{2}=t+1\longrightarrow\infty .
$$

Since $S_{t}\uparrow S_{\infty}$ a.s., monotone convergence gives
${\mathbb E}S_{\infty}=\lim_{t}{\mathbb E}S_{t}=+\infty$.  Hence
$S_{t}$ cannot be $L^{1}$-bounded, let alone $L^{1}$-convergent; in fact

$$
{\mathbb E}|S_{t}-S_{\infty}|\ge {\mathbb E}S_{\infty}-{\mathbb E}S_{t}\to\infty .
$$

${\mathbb E}[(\sigma_{t}^{2})^{2}]=(1+2/(n-1))^{t}\to\infty$.  In
particular the martingale $\sigma_{t}^{2}$ is not uniformly integrable
and ${\mathbb E}\sigma_{t}^{2}\to{\mathbb E}\sigma_{\infty}^{2}=0$ would
require $L^{1}$ convergence, which fails.  This is the usual
``martingale–variance collapse’’: a.s. the estimated variance is driven to
zero geometrically fast, so the partial sums of the variances stay finite
a.s. but their means blow up linearly in $t$. ∎
